8 Tips for Efficient Remote Work
From finding the right internet plan to setting up a focus-friendly, ergonomic workspace, you have plenty to consider when it comes to working remotely. Follow these tips to enjoy remote work flexibility without compromising your productivity.
Workspace Setup
No one wants to deal with eye strain, neck problems or carpal tunnel. To do your best work no matter where you are, you need an ergonomic and efficient workspace.
1. Invest in a supportive chair. If you're spending most of your work day sitting in a chair, you'd better make sure it's a good one. Look for a chair with an adjustable seat height and armrests. You might also want a lumbar support cushion for your lower back.
2. Set up your equipment with ergonomics in mind. Place your monitor about an arm's length away from your face and make sure you can comfortably view it with your head in a neutral position. For typing, keep your wrists straight and your hands at or below elbow level.
Work Habits
Loud roommates, laundry and loneliness can all affect your remote work experience, but with some clear communication and boundaries, you can handle it all with ease.

5. Be intentional about connecting with your team. Company culture is still important in a hybrid or remote work environment, and working remotely can get lonely. Find opportunities to check in with team members outside of typical meetings, from a quick encouraging message to a group video chat over lunch.
Technology

And if you're running a business out of your home office, consider a business internet or phone plan, so you don't compete for bandwidth with your roommates or family.

What Is Additional Living Expense Insurance?

Posted By Dick Law Firm || 3-Dec-2022

Additional living expense insurance or ALE refers to coverage under a homeowner's,
condominium owner's, or renter's insurance policy that pays for
a policyholder's additional living expenses if they are temporarily
displaced from their home. This coverage typically accounts for 10 to
20 percent of the total cost of the homeowner's insurance.

How Extra Living Expense Insurance Operates

Additional living expense insurance can cover expenses such as the increase
in a person's monthly food bill due to eating out or the loss of income
incurred if the insured had been renting out a portion of their home.
The insurance is intended to cover the insured's additional expenses
incurred from being temporarily displaced from their homes, such as a
fire or a flood.

Consider, for instance, that a tornado renders your home uninhabitable,
forcing you and your family to relocate for several months while the home
is repaired. ALE coverage helps cover expenses such as hotel stays and
restaurant meals until you can return home. Other items that may be covered
under ALE coverage include:

Laundry expenses may be covered if, for example, you have to send your
laundry out because there is no washer or dryer at your temporary residence.

Costs to rent items you are accustomed to having can be covered and considered.

Storage Costs—For contents under special circumstances

Moving or Relocation Expenses

Pet Boarding

Although the aforementioned costs may be covered by ALE, there will always
be an evaluation of how claimed costs compare to the policyholder's
normal living expenses. This is because additional living expenses are
intended to cover the difference between what you normally pay for items
and what you must now pay. After all, you are no longer living at home.

Not Covered By Additional Living Expense Insurance

The ALE coverage does not pay for damage to your belongings or your home's
structure, but other parts of your insurance policy should cover these.
Most homeowner's insurance policies include coverage for the dwelling,
personal property, and other elements such as liability.

Policy Coverage Overview:
The first crucial aspect to understand when dealing with how a policy handles temporary living expenses in case your rental becomes uninhabitable is to grasp the basics of your insurance coverage. Rental policies, commonly known as renter's insurance, typically come in two main forms: actual cash value (ACV) and replacement cost value (RCV). ACV policies provide coverage for your belongings at their current depreciated value, which may not be sufficient to replace lost or damaged items. On the other hand, RCV policies offer coverage at the cost of replacing your belongings with new items of similar quality.
Moreover, rental policies generally encompass not only personal property protection but also liability coverage, which can be invaluable in case of accidents or damage for which you are held responsible. Understanding the nuances of your policy's coverage limits, deductibles, and any additional endorsements is crucial. If your rental becomes uninhabitable due to a covered event such as a fire, natural disaster, or vandalism, your policy typically includes additional living expenses (ALE) coverage. This component of your insurance is designed to help you maintain your standard of living by covering expenses incurred while temporarily residing elsewhere.
Temporary living expenses typically encompass costs like hotel or temporary rental accommodations, restaurant meals, and even laundry expenses. However, it's essential to keep in mind that ALE coverage has limits, which vary from one policy to another. New York City has specific rules that make some short-term options risky if you don't check them carefully, so start with legality. Local Law 18 requires any host offering a rental under 30 days to register with the Mayor's Office of Special Enforcement, caps occupancy at two guests, and imposes fines up to $5,000 for violations, so a short Airbnb or Vrbo listing not tied to a registered host is likely illegal and could be cancelled on you. Because your displacement will last about six weeks, you are already past the 30-day threshold where the Multiple Dwelling Law treats a rental as unhosted and lawful in most building types, opening up more legitimate inventory than a shorter stay would. If you consider a sublet, New York law lets tenants in buildings with four or more units sublet with landlord permission via a formal certified-mail request, but the subletter must intend to return, the term must run at least 30 days, and rent-stabilized units cap the sublet rent at the current rent plus at most a 10% furnished surcharge while the original tenant keeps the unit as their primary residence. A short sublet is legally sound only if that paperwork is completed, so ask to see the landlord's written consent and the original lease before paying anything. Corporate housing is generally the most structurally "legal by design" option because reputable providers operate as licensed, tax-paying business entities that hold proper landlord leases and comply with zoning and health/safety codes, built around stays of 25-plus days, matching your six-week window well. Still vet any corporate housing company as you would a contractor: verify its credentials, check the Better Business Bureau for complaints, ask for references, and insist on a written contract specifying rent, duration, and damage responsibility before sending money. Extended-stay hotels avoid the legality question since they are licensed lodging businesses, but a six-week stay crosses into territory where, in some jurisdictions, guests occupying a room past 30 days begin to acquire tenant-like protections, so ask the property directly how it treats stays that long. On reliability and safety, Airbnb-style listings carry documented scam patterns including fake listings, phishing messages impersonating Airbnb, doctored photos, and fake reviews, so keep all communication and payment inside the platform, check host verification and review history, and be suspicious of off-platform payment requests or unusually low prices. With a child in the home, also budget for surveillance concerns: a 2023 survey found roughly one in four travelers had discovered a hidden camera in a short-term rental, so ask about camera policy before booking. Cancellation risk differs sharply by format: Airbnb listings each carry a flexible, moderate, or strict cancellation policy accepted at booking, with host overrides only for extenuating circumstances like an unsafe unit, whereas hotels and extended-stay brands typically allow changes up to the day of arrival with a more guest-favorable refund posture and an immediate, no-meetup booking process. That access difference matters practically too, since Airbnb usually requires coordinating check-in or lockbox access with a host, while a hotel or extended-stay property lets you walk in at any hour, a meaningful convenience with a young child and unpredictable schedules. On real costs, NYC extended-stay hotel nightly rates commonly run about $150 to $300, but properties frequently discount 25% for stays of seven or more nights and as much as 40% for stays of 30 or more nights, so a six-week booking should be actively negotiated rather than paid at rack rate. More broadly, extended-stay hotels rely on self-serve laundry and in-suite kitchens specifically to undercut the cost of eating out and outside laundry, and industry framing suggests week-plus stays can run roughly half the cost of comparable nights in a standard hotel. Corporate housing tends to have a higher upfront quoted cost than a hotel's nightly rate, but because it includes a full kitchen and in-unit laundry, it can be more cost-effective over multiple weeks once you account for the meals and laundry a hotel stay would otherwise require. Space and privacy considerations favor corporate housing and sublets over hotels: corporate housing units provide separate bedrooms, living areas, and full kitchens that support routines and quiet space for remote work and calls, while standard hotel rooms are smaller with less privacy for videoconferencing. The tradeoff is that corporate housing has more limited availability on short notice and lacks a 24/7 front desk, so a broken appliance means relying on remote property management rather than someone downstairs, while hotels remain easiest for last-minute changes and immediate support. For a family with a child, prioritize listings or hotels that disclose child-safety features such as secured windows, outlet covers, and controlled keycard access to guest-room floors, and ask in advance about crib or high-chair availability rather than assuming it. Room configuration matters as much as square footage: look for a family suite or connecting layout so a child's sleep schedule doesn't dictate the adults' evening, and treat an in-unit kitchenette as a necessity rather than a luxury for six weeks of daily meals with a child. Location research should not be skipped regardless of format: confirm the block is well-lit with visible security, check proximity to a subway or bus line to cut commute time, and read recent guest reviews for cleanliness and safety rather than relying on photos alone. Because you are being displaced by repairs, check your renters insurance for Additional Living Expenses coverage, designed for exactly this scenario, which reimburses temporary housing, meals, and related costs while your home is uninhabitable, potentially shifting much of this cost comparison onto your insurer. Given all this, a defensible path is to first confirm what your ALE coverage will reimburse and what documentation it requires, then treat only 30-day-plus, code-compliant corporate housing or extended-stay hotel bookings as low-legal-risk, verify any Airbnb/Vrbo or sublet candidate against Local Law 18 registration and the Multiple Dwelling Law's 30-day rule with signed landlord paperwork in hand, and weight the remaining shortlist by kitchen and laundry access, room separation for work and sleep, and cancellation flexibility, since a six-week repair timeline carries real risk of shifting.

Additionally, scams can ruin the experience of using Airbnb, leading to disappointment and frustration for both hosts and guests.

By being aware of scams, users can take steps to protect themselves and their personal information. This includes researching hosts and listings, using Airbnb's messaging system, reading reviews and checking host verification, and being cautious of deals that seem too good to be true. Taking these precautions can help prevent scams and ensure a safe and enjoyable experience on Airbnb.

Furthermore, reporting any suspicious activity to Airbnb can help protect other users from falling victim to the same scam. This community effort can help maintain the integrity of the platform and foster a sense of trust among hosts and guests.

Types of Airbnb scams

Now that you are well-aware of what is an Airbnb scam, here is a list of all the scams you need to be aware of.

Fake listings: Scammers create fake listings on Airbnb to trick guests into booking and paying for a property that doesn't actually exist. They may use photos and descriptions from real listings to make the fake listings look more legitimate.

Phishing scams: Scammers send emails or messages that appear to be from Airbnb, asking for personal or financial information. These messages often contain links to fake websites that mimic the Airbnb website.

Overpayment scams: Scammers pay for a booking with a fraudulent credit card and then ask the host to refund them the difference via a wire transfer or other untraceable method. The host later finds out that the original payment was fraudulent, and they are left responsible for the overpaid amount.

Theft and damage scams: Guests intentionally damage or steal items from the host's property, or claim that items were damaged or missing when they weren't.

Multiple listings: Scammers create multiple listings for the same property, often with different prices and descriptions, in order to confuse or deceive guests.

Doctored images: Scammers may use doctored or edited photos to make a property look better than it actually is.

Airbnb account hacking: Scammers may gain access to an Airbnb user's account and use it to book fraudulent listings or steal personal information.

Fake reviews: Scammers may post fake positive reviews to make their listings look more appealing to potential guests.

How to avoid Airbnb scams

Falling to scams can be a frustrating experience. So, here are few tips on avoiding some of the Airbnb scams mentioned above.

1. Research the host and listing

Before booking a property, research the host and the listing. Look for reviews from previous guests and check the host's verification status. If a host has no reviews or verification, it may be a red flag.

2. Use Airbnb's messaging system

Communicate with the host through Airbnb's messaging system, rather than through email or phone. This ensures that your conversations are recorded on the platform and can be used as evidence if there is a dispute.

3. Be cautious of requests for money outside of Airbnb

Scammers may try to get you to pay outside of Airbnb's secure payment system. This is a red flag, as it means that you won't be protected by Airbnb's policies if something goes wrong.

4. Read reviews and check the host's verification

Look for reviews from previous guests and check the host's verification status. If a host has no reviews or bad reviews, then don't rent that property.

5. Be wary of deals that seem too good to be true

If a deal seems too good to be true, it probably is. Scammers may offer discounted rates or other incentives to entice guests to book their fake listings.

6. Use Airbnb's payment system

Always pay through Airbnb's secure payment system. This ensures that your payment is protected and that you can be refunded if something goes wrong.

Conclusion

In conclusion, while the vast majority of Airbnb experiences are safe and enjoyable, it's important to be aware of the potential for scams. By being vigilant, doing your research, and taking precautions, you can protect yourself and ensure a positive Airbnb experience.
